  "candidates": [
    {
      "startEvent": 424,
      "endEvent": 434,
      "contextStartEvent": 397,
      "contextEndEvent": 450,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "We wouldn't do that. They would leave it to the religious to do it",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "The categorical secular/religious contrast supplies an assurance that secularists never desecrate. Neither the appeal to ordinary morality and Antigone (E428–E432) nor examples of religious violence establish that exclusion. Hitchens qualifies which religious group behaves best (E443–E447), but does not qualify secular immunity or explicitly neutralize contrary evidence."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1379,
      "endEvent": 1383,
      "contextStartEvent": 1204,
      "contextEndEvent": 1410,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "those who run orphanages say nothing and prove nothing about their religion.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The dismissal could exclude charitable outcomes from evaluating religious influence regardless of merits. However, Hitchens supplies secular parallels, distinguishes charity from religious justification, and also declines to blame Christianity for abuse (E1284–E1294, E1373–E1383). Whether he excludes relevant causal evidence or only rejects proof of religious truth remains ambiguous."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1746,
      "endEvent": 1766,
      "contextStartEvent": 1665,
      "contextEndEvent": 1766,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "it only makes sense if we see it in context as part of an overarching cosmic war",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["fear"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The cosmic-war framing and appeal to divine credibility could shelter civilian killing through unseen purposes. Yet Olasky offers a recognizable wartime-necessity analogy, acknowledges horror, and leaves comparable decisions debatable (E1693–E1741). He does not explicitly say every divine action must be justified, so unconditional protection is uncertain."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1852,
      "endEvent": 1857,
      "contextStartEvent": 1822,
      "contextEndEvent": 1858,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Do you want to separate the two? You know, impossible.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["ridicule"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Olasky adopts a quoted association of faith and charity and calls separation impossible. His Katrina examples support religious charitable activity, not its necessary dependence on faith. The intended scope is uncertain: he later recognizes secular giving and invokes common grace (E2575–E2579, E2855–E2861), rather than denying all nonreligious charity."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2032,
      "endEvent": 2033,
      "contextStartEvent": 1997,
      "contextEndEvent": 2089,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "If you want to get good people to do wicked things, you need religion.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["shame"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Hitchens endorses Weinberg's maxim and supplies circumcision and religiously sanctioned discrimination as illustrations (E2034–E2086). Those examples explain a possible route from good intentions to harmful conduct, but do not establish religion as necessary. The maxim carries that unsupported exclusivity; no device makes contrary cases inadmissible."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2126,
      "endEvent": 2137,
      "contextStartEvent": 2097,
      "contextEndEvent": 2139,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "you've proved absolutely nothing at all.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After acknowledging the driver's Muslim motivation (E2111–E2112), Hitchens treats religious attribution as polluting the act and dismisses its evidential contribution. This may insulate his moral indictment from beneficial religious motivation. His stated alternative—that returning money already has sufficient ordinary moral reasons—also supports a narrower objection to theological inference."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2167,
      "endEvent": 2174,
      "contextStartEvent": 2164,
      "contextEndEvent": 2175,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Why should we believe it at all? It's it's a random utterance.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["none"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Olasky gives an ordinary, though unsupported, inference from contingent existence to unreliable speech; he does not merely replace reasoning with a catchphrase. Its protective use is explicit: anything Hitchens says becomes untrustworthy because of his account of origins (E2167–E2174), without considering the particular claim's evidence or reasoning."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2845,
      "endEvent": 2847,
      "contextStartEvent": 2782,
      "contextEndEvent": 2850,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "only religion can make people act in a bad way in such a circumstance.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "This renewed exclusivity claim follows the Good Samaritan discussion and an alleged religious permission to withhold aid (E2818–E2843). These supply reasons that humane action needs no Christian instruction and that religious rules can obstruct it. They do not establish that religion alone can cause harmful conduct in that circumstance."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2855,
      "endEvent": 2872,
      "contextStartEvent": 2767,
      "contextEndEvent": 2894,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "are we living off the interest at that point?",
      "form": "unclear",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Common grace and inherited moral resources answer the challenge of nonreligious goodness. They might absorb counterexamples to religion's necessity without independent support, but Olasky calls grace only one explanation and poses cultural depletion as a question (E2859–E2872). The text does not establish an unrestricted dismissal of contrary evidence."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 479,
      "endEvent": 507,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "Mr. Jefferson build up that wall.",
      "explanation": "Although expressly called a slogan, it summarizes the church–state separation argument: interdenominational conflict, the Danbury example, and proposed religious restrictions supply its practical rationale (E466–E503). Its brevity does not replace missing reasons."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2438,
      "endEvent": 2445,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "I'm obviously not saying that only Christians or religious people have long marriages",
      "explanation": "Olasky limits his marriage testimony to his own experience, connecting the antidote metaphor to a described personal change (E2426–E2447). The causal testimony is contestable, but the qualification prevents treating this passage as an unsupported assertion that only Christians can sustain marriages."
    }
  ]
